title: The dancer who bows out
hook: a dancer leaves the stage once she's been seen, and the Yoga Sutras end on one small word
carry: kaivalya: the seer resting in itself
tomorrow: The question that starts the Ramayana

segments.voice: Yesterday: klesha. Yashoda saw the universe when the covering came off. Knowledge was covered, never small.

Samkhya, Yoga's sister school, tells its whole philosophy as a little drama. There's a watcher, who can see but can't move, and a dancer, who can move but can't see for herself: nature, with all its colors. The two need each other, the old text says, like a lame man riding on a blind man's shoulders through a forest. So the dancer dances: the world, the body, every thought and mood, a whole show for one watcher. And once she knows she has truly been seen, she stops. She bows out, and never shows herself to him again.
screen: `A WATCHER WHO CAN'T MOVE.` → `A DANCER WHO CAN'T SEE.` → `A WHOLE SHOW FOR ONE WATCHER.` → `ONCE SEEN, SHE BOWS OUT.`

segments.voice: Patanjali's last sutras tell the same ending. Sutra 4.32: then, their purpose fulfilled, the gunas finish their sequence of change. The gunas are the three strands of nature, what the mind and the world are woven from. Nature has danced for a reason, Patanjali said back in sutra 2.18: to give the seer experience, and then freedom. Purpose served, the dance stops. Sutra 4.33 adds that change is grasped at the end of a transformation, the way you notice a child has grown when the old shoes don't fit. Then the last thread, 4.34: purushartha-shunyanam gunanam pratiprasavah kaivalyam, svarupa-pratishtha va chiti-shaktir iti. Kaivalya is the gunas returning to their source, with nothing left to do for the seer. Or: the power of consciousness, resting in its own nature. Thus. This is the goal Hindus call moksha, freedom from the round of birth and death. Each school names it its own way; Yoga's name is kaivalya, consciousness no longer mistaken for the dance. And the book closes on iti, thus, the word Sanskrit uses to end a quotation or a whole work. Fifty-nine days ago this block opened on atha, now. All four chapters, from the top. Samadhi Pada: stilling the mind's turnings. Sadhana Pada: the practice and the eight limbs. Vibhuti Pada: the powers, and the warning about them. Kaivalya Pada: the mind seen clearly, and set down. Most days we live inside the show: the feed, the mood, the mind performing. The tradition's last word on it is gentle. The show is real, and you were the one it was danced for.
screen: `THE DANCE HAS A PURPOSE.` · `THE GUNAS' WORK IS DONE.` · `KAIVALYA: YOGA'S NAME FOR MOKSHA.` · `FROM NOW TO THUS.` · then, large: `KAIVALYA: THE SEER RESTING IN ITSELF.`

segments.voice: For this last sit with Patanjali, do less than ever: let the body be held, let the breath happen without you, and let thoughts be the gunas finishing their work. You aren't reaching for anything; you're resting in what was already here. If you pray, you can offer these sixty days to God, in whatever words are your own.
Kaivalya. In the last thread: the gunas gone back to their source, and the power of consciousness resting in its own nature, the goal the whole Yoga Sutras points toward.
Your line: kaivalya, the seer resting in itself. The dancer has bowed. Tomorrow, a new story begins in a forest: the Ramayana.

screen: `DAY 489 COUNTS.` → `THE YOGA SUTRAS, DONE: SIXTY SESSIONS.` → `TOMORROW: THE QUESTION THAT STARTS THE RAMAYANA.`

howItsDone: Many students of the Yoga Sutras finish a reading of the text by chanting its last sutra, and teachers describe kaivalya as consciousness abiding in its own nature, no longer identified with the mind.

chat.meaning: Sutra 4.34: kaivalya is the gunas returning to their source, or consciousness resting in its own nature. In the Samkhya Karika, nature dances for the seer and stops once she's been seen. Hindus call the goal moksha.
